I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was this really tall woman who always wore these bright floral dresses, and she had this huge collection of ceramic owls on her desk. I don't know why owls, maybe she just liked them, but one of them had a chipped beak from when Tommy Henderson knocked it over during indoor recess. Anyway, she was always having to remind me to finish my classwork, and I was notorious for leaving my homework shoved in the back of my desk. My desk was always a disaster zone, honestly. I’d find assignments from a month ago crammed in next to my math book.\n\nDoctor: Do these attention problems affect you at work, too?\n\nPatient: Well, I'm actually not working right now. Lately I’ve been forgetting things I really meant to do. Like, just last week, I was supposed to return a call from the doctor’s office—my primary care guy, Dr. Evans. She always wears these huge, colorful statement necklaces. I don't know where she finds them, probably at those little artisan craft fairs they have downtown on the weekends. He’s got this old Buick, a '98 LeSabre, and the passenger side door sticks, so you have to yank it just right to get it open. Fidgety? No, I don't think so. I was actually a pretty quiet kid. I'd just sit at my desk, mostly. I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was incredibly strict, so you didn't dare get out of your seat in her room anyway. Smithson's was this big lumber yard on the edge of town, right next to the railroad tracks. We used to walk down there in the summer and put pennies on the tracks to let the freight trains flatten them out. You had to be quick about it, though, because the switch operator would yell at you if he caught you trespassing. Oh, absolutely. It's a daily struggle. I'm always putting down my keys, or my phone, or the garden clippers somewhere in the house and then I end up spending ten minutes just retracing my steps to find them. Or those catering receipts! Careless mistakes? Hmm. No, I don't really think so. I actually took a lot of pride in my assignments back then, especially my handwriting. We had to learn cursive, you know, the Palmer Method, and the teacher made us do these endless loops on our lined paper. He was a real stickler for penmanship.

Well, at home... I mean, my parents definitely knew about it, mostly because they heard it from the school. Even back in grade school, you know, way before I was 12, the teachers were always telling my parents that I was a bright kid, but I was just constantly daydreaming. 

I'd be staring out the window, probably thinking about those model airplanes I used to build. I had this whole fleet of balsa wood planes. You had to use this special model cement, smelled incredibly strong, but it held those tiny little wooden wing ribs together perfectly. My dad helped me hang them from my bedroom ceiling with fishing line so they looked like they were flying. He used this old metal step stool to reach the ceiling, and it had one wheel that squeaked so loudly it would drive my mother absolutely crazy. She eventually gave that stool away to our neighbor, Mr. Henderson. He spent all his time out in his greenhouse trying to grow prize-winning beefsteak tomatoes. He actually won a blue ribbon at the county fair one year, if you can believe it. He used this special fertilizer made from seaweed or something.

But, uh, anyway... my parents. Right. The teachers told them I was always daydreaming, and that I was always leaving my homework stuffed inside my desk. We had those heavy wooden desks where the whole top lifted up on hinges, and I'd just shove everything in there and completely forget about it. And they said I always needed reminders just to finish my regular classwork. So, even if I wasn't doing the work at home, my parents definitely knew I wasn't paying attention.

Trouble following what they were saying? No, I don't think so. We usually talked the most during dinner, and I could follow along just fine. Every night at six o'clock sharp, we'd sit down. We had this big, heavy oak table that my grandfather actually built by hand. 

He was a master carpenter, worked for the railway for, gosh, almost forty years. He helped lay down tracks all over the state. But, uh... yeah, to answer your question, I didn't really have a problem following my parents when they talked to me at the house. I heard them just fine.
